Question seven. What is model quantization? Storing the weights in fewer bits: eight-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats, or even four bits. The model gets smaller, moves less data through memory, and usually runs faster. Take a small neural network that reads handwritten digits. Its seventeen thousand weights take sixty-eight kilobytes as 32-bit floats, and it gets ninety-seven point eight percent of five hundred forty held-out digits right. Round every weight to eight bits, a quarter of the size, and not one answer changes. At four bits, an eighth of the size, accuracy still holds. At two, it collapses to twenty-nine percent. Rounding a finished model is post-training quantization: simple, and often enough. For aggressive compression, quantization-aware training rounds during training, so the weights learn to tolerate it. Either way, compare answers, not just the average: at four bits, two answers changed, one fixed and one broken, and accuracy didn't move. Speed is half the job. The system also has to learn whether the model was right.

Question eight. What is label collection, and how do feedback loops work? After launch, the label is the outcome the prediction led to: a click, a purchase, a confirmed fraud. Logging it beside the prediction closes the loop. Three things bend that loop. Labels arrive late: a purchase days after the click. You only see outcomes the model let happen: a transaction it blocked never shows whether it was fraud. And its actions change the data it sees next. So log what the model decided, not just the outcome, and keep a small random slice where it doesn't decide. Those outcomes are the only ones the model didn't choose.
